difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: a single-step computation with one formula, z = (v − mean)/standard deviation, where the only care needed is to ignore the minimum and maximum; under a minute for a prepared student.
stem: Let the minimum, maximum, mean and standard deviation values for the attribute *income* of data scientists be ₹46000, ₹170000, ₹96000, and ₹21000, respectively. The $z$-score normalized *income* value of ₹106000 is closest to which **ONE** of the following options?

solution.quick: $z$-score normalization uses only the mean and the standard deviation: $z = \dfrac{v - \mu}{\sigma} = \dfrac{106000 - 96000}{21000} = \dfrac{10}{21} \approx 0.476$, option **(B)**. The minimum and maximum are not needed; they belong to min–max normalization.

steps.title: Formula and the values it needs
steps.body:
$z$-score (zero-mean) normalization maps a value $v$ of attribute $A$ to

$$
v' = \frac{v - \mu_A}{\sigma_A},
$$

where $\mu_A$ is the mean and $\sigma_A$ the standard deviation of $A$. From the stem:

- $v = 106000$
- $\mu_A = 96000$
- $\sigma_A = 21000$

The minimum (₹46000) and maximum (₹170000) do not appear in this formula.

steps.title: Substitute and calculate
steps.body:
$$
v' = \frac{106000 - 96000}{21000} = \frac{10000}{21000} = \frac{10}{21} = 0.47619\ldots \approx 0.476.
$$

The rupees cancel, so the normalized value is a pure number. It says that an income of ₹106000 lies $0.476$ standard deviations **above** the mean.

steps.title: Why the other options do not fit
steps.body:
None of the other options equals $(v - \mu_A)/\sigma_A$. For reference, each lies close to a quotient that mixes up the given statistics (the paper does not say how its options were built; this only shows which slips land near them):

| Option | Value | Nearby wrong computation |
|---|---|---|
| (A) | 0.217 | $\dfrac{106000 - 96000}{46000} = 0.2174$: dividing the deviation by the minimum instead of $\sigma$ |
| (C) | 0.623 | $\dfrac{106000}{170000} = 0.6235$: dividing the raw value by the maximum, with no mean subtracted |
| (D) | 2.304 | $\dfrac{106000}{46000} = 2.3043$: dividing the raw value by the minimum |

Min–max normalization to $[0, 1]$ would give $\dfrac{106000 - 46000}{170000 - 46000} = \dfrac{60000}{124000} \approx 0.484$. That is not one of the options (its nearest option happens to be (B) as well), and it is not what the question asks for. The $z$-score is $10/21 \approx 0.476$.

solution.teaching:
**Why normalize?** Attributes measured on different scales (income in lakhs, age in years, rating from 1 to 5) would let the large-valued attribute dominate distance-based methods such as $k$-NN, $k$-means or gradient-based training. Normalization rescales attribute values to a common range. Three standard methods from data preprocessing:

**1. Min–max normalization** maps $[\min_A, \max_A]$ linearly onto a new range $[\text{new\_min}, \text{new\_max}]$:

$$
v' = \frac{v - \min_A}{\max_A - \min_A}\,(\text{new\_max} - \text{new\_min}) + \text{new\_min}.
$$

It needs the minimum and maximum, and a single outlier squeezes all the other values together.

**2. $z$-score (zero-mean) normalization** centres by the mean and scales by the standard deviation:

$$
v' = \frac{v - \mu_A}{\sigma_A}.
$$

After this transformation the attribute has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. A value's $z$-score tells you how many standard deviations it lies above (positive) or below (negative) the mean. It is useful when the true min and max are unknown or when outliers would dominate min–max scaling.

**3. Decimal scaling** divides by a power of ten, $v' = v / 10^j$, where $j$ is the smallest integer that makes $\max |v'| < 1$.

**Back to this question.** The stem deliberately lists all four summary statistics. The name of the method, "$z$-score", tells you which two to use: the mean ₹96000 and the standard deviation ₹21000. The income ₹106000 is ₹10000 above the mean, and ₹10000 is $10/21 \approx 0.476$ of one standard deviation.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $0.217$ is not $(v - \mu)/\sigma$; it matches $\dfrac{106000 - 96000}{46000} = 0.2174$, i.e. dividing the deviation from the mean by the **minimum** instead of the standard deviation. The $z$-score divides by $\sigma = 21000$, giving $0.476$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $z = \dfrac{106000 - 96000}{21000} = \dfrac{10}{21} = 0.47619\ldots$, which rounds to $0.476$. This matches the official key.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $0.623$ is not $(v - \mu)/\sigma$; it lies close to $\dfrac{106000}{170000} = 0.6235$, the raw value divided by the **maximum** with no mean subtracted. That is a max-scaling, not a $z$-score.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $2.304$ matches $\dfrac{106000}{46000} = 2.3043$, the raw value divided by the **minimum**. A $z$-score of $2.304$ would mean the income lies $2.3$ standard deviations above the mean, i.e. near $96000 + 2.304 \times 21000 \approx 144384$, but ₹106000 is only ₹10000 (less than half a standard deviation) above the mean.

solution.shortcut: Ignore min and max; compute $(v - \mu)/\sigma = 10000/21000 = 10/21$. Since $1/21 \approx 0.0476$, $10/21 \approx 0.476$.
solution.commonTrap: Reaching for the minimum and maximum just because they are given. They belong to min–max normalization, $\dfrac{106000 - 46000}{170000 - 46000} \approx 0.484$, which is a different transformation (here its nearest option happens to be (B) too, so the slip is conceptual rather than costly, but on a question with closer options it would be). Mixing min or max into the $z$-score formula produces numbers like those in options (A), (C) and (D). A $z$-score needs only the mean and the standard deviation.

transcription.notes: Transcribed from the official paper rendering and independently checked against it. The rupee amounts are written with the ₹ symbol and without thousands separators, exactly as printed (₹46000, ₹170000, ₹96000, ₹21000, ₹106000). The attribute name income is italic in the paper (both occurrences), and the italic z of "z-score" is written as $z$. The options are plain decimals, as printed. No figure is needed; the region contains only text and the GATE 2024 background watermark.

answerVerification.method: Blind independent re-solve + Python check agrees with official key
answerVerification.checkCode:
mn, mx, mean, sd, x = 46000, 170000, 96000, 21000, 106000
z = (x - mean) / sd
opts = {'A': 0.217, 'B': 0.476, 'C': 0.623, 'D': 2.304}
best = min(opts, key=lambda k: abs(opts[k] - z))
print('z-score =', round(z, 5), '-> closest', best); assert best == 'B'
print('min-max =', round((x - mn) / (mx - mn), 5))
print('(x-mean)/min =', round((x - mean) / mn, 4), ' x/max =', round(x / mx, 4), ' x/min =', round(x / mn, 4))
answerVerification.notes: Independent verifier solved blind before consulting the key: z = (106000 − 96000)/21000 = 10/21 ≈ 0.47619, closest to option B (0.476, distance ≈ 0.0002; next closest C at ≈ 0.147). Minimum and maximum are not used by z-score normalization. The Python check (re-run by the verifier) also shows the other option values lie near (106000 − 96000)/46000 ≈ 0.2174 (A), 106000/170000 ≈ 0.6235 (C) and 106000/46000 ≈ 2.3043 (D); these are only presented as plausible slips, not as the paper's construction. Min–max normalization would give ≈ 0.4839, not an option. Agrees with official key B.
